--- FILE: .plaesy/spec/sourdough-office-bakery/spec.md ---
# Spec: Sourdough Bakery for Office Sales

Status: draft
Topic: sourdough-office-bakery

## Purpose

Establish a sourdough bread bakery that produces and delivers premium, fresh sourdough loaves directly to offices within a single city. The business targets office managers and corporate purchasers seeking daily or weekly bread supplies, competing on quality and convenience rather than price. Success depends on reliable daily production, efficient delivery logistics, customer acquisition in the B2B office market, and margins sufficient to sustain operations with a small initial team.

## Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Acceptance criterion (Given / When / Then) | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Supply and production capability | Given sourced ingredients (flour, water, salt, starter culture) at sustainable prices, when daily production begins, then 30+ loaves are produced daily at consistent quality and cost | open |
| R2 | B2B revenue from office customers | Given identified office customer segments, when agreements are signed, then revenue from bread sales reaches $5,000/month by month 6 | open |
| R3 | Delivery logistics and freshness guarantee | Given confirmed delivery routes and office locations, when bread is baked, then loaves are delivered within 8 hours of baking to maintain freshness claims | open |
| R4 | Market differentiation and positioning | Given competitive analysis of local bread vendors, when marketing begins, then messaging and pricing establish sourdough quality as the primary value (not convenience or lowest cost) | open |
| R5 | Food safety and regulatory compliance | Given production facility in place, when inspections occur, then all local food safety, labeling, and business licensing requirements are met | open |
| R6 | Profitability and unit economics | Given production and delivery costs calculated, when sales reach $10,000/month, then gross margin is ≥40% and operating margin is ≥15% | open |
| R7 | Customer retention and repeat orders | Given first 20 office customers acquired, when orders are tracked, then at least 70% of customers place repeat orders within 60 days | open |
| R8 | Production consistency and quality control | Given standard recipes and baking procedures, when loaves are produced, then >95% pass quality inspection (appearance, weight, crumb structure, crust color) | open |

## Non-goals

- Distribution outside a single city
- Retail storefront or consumer walk-in sales (B2C)
- Specialty breads beyond sourdough (no focaccia, rye, or gluten-free variants in v1)
- Catering or large events
- Online direct-to-consumer shipping
- Organic or heirloom grain certification (can add later if demand emerges)

## Open questions

- UNKNOWN: Total addressable market in the city. How many offices are there, and what percentage buy fresh bread regularly? Owner: Market research
- UNKNOWN: Customer acquisition cost. What marketing spend per office is required to close a contract? Owner: Sales & marketing
- UNKNOWN: Capital requirements. How much inventory, equipment, and working capital is needed to launch and sustain 6 months? Owner: Finance
- ASSUMED — Wholesale price point: $5–7 per loaf sold to offices, vs. $10+ retail in cafes. Confirmed through competitive pricing survey of local bakeries.
- ASSUMED — Delivery frequency: Most offices want 2–3 deliveries per week. To be validated with early customer interviews.
- ASSUMED — Production scale: One baker can produce 30–50 loaves daily in a shared commercial kitchen or dedicated space. To be tested in prototype phase.
- ASSUMED — Minimum order: Offices must commit to at least 5 loaves per delivery to justify logistics cost. To be flexible in early sales.

## Risks and assumptions

**Market risks:**
- Offices may have existing relationships with bakeries or catering suppliers; switching cost and buyer inertia are high.
- Demand may be seasonal (lower bread consumption in summer if offices are in vacation mode).

**Operational risks:**
- Daily production is inflexible; unsold loaves represent waste and margin loss.
- Delivery logistics can become expensive if office density is low or spread across the city.
- Food safety incident (contamination, illness) could destroy brand and business.

**Competitive risks:**
- Established local bakeries or national chains (Panera, Boulud) may offer sourdough; competing on price is not viable.
- Coffee shops and corporate cafeterias increasingly bake fresh bread in-house.

**Assumptions:**
- Sourdough is perceived as premium and worth 2–3× the price of supermarket bread by office buyers.
- A small team (one baker + one deliveries/sales person) can sustain the business at $10k–15k/month revenue.
- Shared commercial kitchen or dedicated leased space is available at <$1,500/month.

## References

- No external sources cited yet; all requirements and assumptions are hypothetical and require validation.

## Next steps

- Conduct 20+ office manager interviews to validate demand and willingness to pay.
- Map office density and delivery feasibility in the target city.
- Prototype batch baking and cost production.
- Identify and book a commercial kitchen space or lease option.
